newsitem.title: USA: Egypt Air hijacker sentenced to life in U.S..
newsitem.headline: Egypt Air hijacker sentenced to life in U.S..

text.p: A federal judge on Monday sentenced a Palestinian hijacker of a 1985 Egypt Air flight in which 58 people died to life in prison for air piracy.

Prosecutors depicted Omar Mohammed Ali Rezaq, 38, a Lebanese-born Palestinian recruited into the Abu Nidal guerrilla movement, as "a killing machine" and asked U.S. District Court Judge Royce Lamberth for the maximum life sentence. The pilot of the plane testified that he hummed and sang during the bloodbath.

Although Rezaq will be eligible to seek parole after 10 years, Lamberth said he would seek to have him serve the full life sentence. He also ordered Rezaq to pay $264,000 in restitution to some of the victims' families.

At an emotional sentencing hearing, prosecutor Joseph Valder broke down recalling how Rezaq murdered two women by shooting them at point-blank range and a victim's husband denounced the hijacker as "a pitiful murderer."

"You will never be a martyr," said Ed Leonard, an Ontario, Canada man whose wife Belinda and 18-month-old son Andrew died in the hijacking while he waited in vain for them at the airport in Cairo on Nov. 23, 1985.
"You established your own court of lawlessness," Leonard said. "You established yourself as the judge, the jury, the sole executioner" for "a mindless hateful political agenda."

"You will only be one thing: a pitiful murderer condemned to the worst fate of all, living with yourself for the rest of your miserable life," Leonard told Rezaq. He held aloft a penciled drawing he made of Rezaq and told him "the next time I want to see your name is on your obituary."

Rezaq, speaking in fractured English, told the judge in a rambling statement before sentencing that he was a different man than the one who picked out anyone carrying an Israeli or American passport, shot them in the head and shoved their bodies to the tarmac below at the airport in Malta during a refueling stop.
"I don't born to kill ... I ask God to bless all those people. I ask God to make peace in my country. I ask God for peace in Palestine," Rezaq told the judge.

He was convicted of a single air piracy count in July after a trial in which he claimed he became a militant after he was driven from his homeland by Israel and witnessed the horrors of war in the Middle East.
A jury rejected his claim that he was insane when he boarded Flight 648 in Athens, armed with grenades and pistols.
"At one moment, I cannot imagine how to understand," he said. "I don't believe me bad man."
But Valder, standing before the autopsy pictures of the two women Rezaq killed, choked up as he said through the four years he had dealt with the case the photos haunted him.

"I never could accept ... or get past the horrible wrongness ... of a bright, good, kind gentlewoman of 38 years, to see her murdered, a bullet in the middle of her brain, simply because she was an American citizen," Valder said.
Rezaq was convicted of murder in 1985 and sentenced to 25 years in jail in Malta, but served only seven years before being released.
U.S. officials arrested him on air piracy charges after he made his way to Nigeria in 1993 and claimed that he was let go when Libya put pressure on Maltese authorities.
